planting.note: Plant container stock in fall to early winter so roots establish before Gulf Coast summer heat arrives.

directions: Summer Sunset is a USDA-ARS rabbiteye release bred specifically as an edible ornamental for home landscapes, with berries that shift through yellow-green, orange-red, and purple before ripening to black within the same cluster. It needs roughly 500 to 550 hours of winter chilling below 45 degrees F, a modest requirement that fits well with Gulf Coast winters, and like other rabbiteye types it sets a heavier crop when a second rabbiteye variety is planted nearby for cross-pollination. Grow it in full sun in well-drained, acidic soil with a pH between 4.5 and 5.5, mulched with pine bark to conserve moisture. Expect spring bloom followed by a long, colorful ripening season into summer, with the plant also valued for its reddish winter stems.

common_name: Cutie Pie Dwarf Southern Highbush Blueberry

planting.note: Container-friendly; plant in fall for root establishment or any time from a nursery pot while avoiding peak summer heat.

directions: Cutie Pie is a compact, container-friendly southern highbush selection bred by Scott NeSmith at the University of Georgia specifically for home landscapes, staying under about 3 to 4 feet tall with a tidy, rounded form. It is self-pollinating, though planting a second southern highbush variety nearby can improve fruit set and berry size. Site it in full sun in moist, acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) amended with peat or pine bark, since its shallow roots dry out quickly in sandy coastal soils. It flowers in early spring with abundant white-pink blossoms and ripens a modest but flavorful crop of small dark berries over an extended window, making it well suited to patio containers as well as small garden beds.
sources: University of Georgia CAES Extension newswire

planting.note: Plant dormant or container stock in fall so roots establish before summer heat and dry spells.

directions: Frostberry Delight is a rabbiteye blueberry bred by Scott NeSmith at the University of Georgia and introduced for its blue-green, almost silvery summer foliage and reddish twigs as much as for its fruit, reaching roughly 4 to 6 feet tall and wide. It requires about 500 to 550 chill hours, comfortably met by most Gulf Coast winters, and yields improve when another rabbiteye cultivar is planted nearby for cross-pollination. Give it full sun and acidic, well-drained soil in the 4.5 to 5.5 pH range, since rabbiteye types tolerate heat and short dry spells better than highbush blueberries once established. Spring flowers give way to large sky-blue berries that ripen over an extended period, and the foliage turns red in fall for added landscape interest beyond the harvest.
sources: University of Georgia CAES Extension newswire

planting.note: Ideal for raised beds or containers; plant from fall through winter for best establishment.

directions: Southern Bluebelle is an ultra-dwarf southern highbush cultivar maturing at only about 2 to 3 feet tall yet still setting a surprisingly heavy crop of medium to large light-blue berries. Its chilling requirement is unusually low, around 250 hours below 45 degrees F, which makes it one of the more forgiving choices for mild Gulf Coast winters that sometimes fall short of what standard highbush types need. Plant it in full sun in consistently moist, acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), and pair it with another southern highbush variety to boost cross-pollination and fruit size. Profuse spring flowering is followed by a generous harvest for such a small plant, making it a good fit for raised beds, foundation plantings, or large containers.
sources: commercial nursery cultivar listings (Burpee, Stark Bro's, The Tree Center)

planting.note: Plant in fall to early winter so the narrow upright bush establishes before its unusually late spring bloom.

directions: Gupton is a southern highbush blueberry released in 2006 by the USDA-ARS Small Fruit Research Station in Poplarville, Mississippi, bred specifically for humid Gulf South conditions and growing into an upright, cone-shaped bush to around 6 feet. It needs only about 400 to 500 chill hours and flowers unusually late relative to other southern highbush types, which helps it dodge the late freezes that can damage earlier-blooming varieties, while still ripening its crop well ahead of the earliest rabbiteye cultivars. Grow it in full sun in moist, acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) with a thick pine-bark or pine-straw mulch; its medium to large, light-blue berries have a high sugar content and resist cracking even after rain near harvest.
sources: USDA-ARS Small Fruit Research Station, Poplarville, MS (ars.usda.gov plant release records)
